note:
The authored key_locations tables that live in Python rather than in catalogue.json or exteriors.json. This is the largest body of un-externalised authored content in the five packages, and two of its tables are RNG-INDEXED.

* `naming.adjectives` -- core/naming.py:15-17 ADJECTIVES. HARD POSITIONAL CONTRACT: fill() does `ADJECTIVES[draw.randrange(len(ADJECTIVES))]` to resolve every `{adj}` placeholder. Reordering this tuple renames locations in every world. `naming.qualifiers` -- core/naming.py:80 QUALIFIERS, iterated IN ORDER by unique_name() to build disambiguating variants, so it too is positional. The source states they are DISJOINT FROM ADJECTIVES ON PURPOSE: an overlap silently shrinks the variant pool and only shows up as a duplicate name once a world is crowded enough to exhaust it. `naming.fallbacks` are the strings fill() substitutes when a context key is missing -- 'the waste', 'the old people', 'unquiet', 'the nameless', 'lone' -- so an ABSENT context value produces authored English, not an empty slot.
* `composition.ordinals` -- core/composition.py:33-34 ORDINALS. POSITIONALLY INDEXED, twelve words; a chain member is named by its place in the chain.
* `succession` -- core/succession.py. `threat_base` maps occupant to a base threat 1-4 on the SAME creature-tier scale the nest catalogue uses (deliberately, so a dungeon and a beast lair are comparable), clamped to min_threat..max_threat = 1..5. `hostile` and `untended_states` are classifications. `state_bends` and `occupant_bends` are the INLINE LITERAL bend tables inside derive_state() and derive_occupant(): the catalogue supplies the weights and this module multiplies them. The multiplications are applied in the listed order and float multiplication is not associative, so keep the order; the subsequent choose() re-sorts the weight keys (`items = sorted(weights.items())`) before its cumulative walk, so the CATALOGUE's dict order is free but THESE factors' order is not.
* `interiors.roles` -- core/interiors.py:24-36 ROLES, 11 families x 4-6 chamber role names, and `plan_notes`, `fallback_roles`, `entrance_kinds`, `flooded_states`, `collapse_states`. `interiors.tuning` holds the biases scattered through that module.
* `vocabularies` -- catalogue.py:12-23, the closed enums the catalogue lint enforces (states, occupants, interior_plans, tiers, domains, placements, along) plus the schema key sets. `exteriors.part_kinds`, `arrangements` and `shapes` are the same for the exterior side. These are what make an unknown value a load failure rather than a silent default.
* `exteriors.ruin_states` -- exteriors.py:110 RUIN_STATES, state -> rubble intensity. ONLY SIX of the catalogue's eleven states are keyed, and a site in one of the other five gets NO weathering parts at all. `rubble_part_id`/`overgrown_part_id` are HARD-CODED PART IDS that must exist in exteriors.json and which nothing validates.
* `exterior.arrangement_draws` -- core/exterior.py:69-124, the NUMBER OF RNG DRAWS each arrangement consumes per part. A port MUST match these exactly, because a wrong draw count desynchronises the whole site stream even where the geometry is unaffected. Note `row` and `courtyard` consume ZERO.
* `placement`, `shaping`, `fields`, `tuning` -- the scoring, terrain-deformation and distance-field constants. `fields.diagonal` IS AN ORDERED 8-NEIGHBOUR STENCIL with sqrt(2) weights and its order is the order the BFS relaxes neighbours in; `golden_angle` (2.39996322972865332) and `surface_posts` (17) drive the scatter arrangement.

RNG INPUT: yes -- `naming.adjectives`, `naming.qualifiers`, `composition.ordinals`, the two bend tables and `exterior.arrangement_draws` all sit directly on the draw path. `key_locations.seeds` is a pure re-export of world_geometry.seeds: sha256('tectonics-v1:{master}:{domain}:{variation}').digest()[:4] read BIG-ENDIAN into random.Random. PORT-CRITICAL: the port must reproduce CPython's Mersenne Twister random(), randint(), randrange() and shuffle() exactly, or none of the order contracts above matter.

IDENTITY HASH: none. key_locations contains no hashlib call.

plan_notes.linear: One way in, one way on; depth is the only axis.
plan_notes.branching: A spine with workings off it, the way anything dug for profit grows.
plan_notes.radial: Built around a centre, with everything else facing it.
plan_notes.warren: Dug without a plan over a long time; loops back on itself.
plan_notes.vault: Shallow and wide: a few large rooms rather than a descent.

interiors.method: Chamber graph only: depth, role, rough size and connections. Plans differ in how chambers attach - linear chains, branching spines, radial hubs, looping warrens, shallow vaults. State decides how much of it is flooded or fallen in.

exteriors.method: One plan per key location, in the local metre frame the city and castle planners already use. A kit resolves per archetype and falls back to its family; parts are shared across kits. Seven arrangement rules place them: a single centred part, a ring, a golden-angle scatter, a row, an inward-facing courtyard, a terrace stepped along the fall of the ground, or a mouth with its approach fanned in front. Ground elevation is sampled at each plot corner, and a location in a ruined or buried state gains rubble in proportion to how far gone it is. Parts that move the ground do so: a barrow is a mound in the terrain, a quarry is a cut, a crater is a rim with a bowl inside it, and plots are seated on the shaped ground rather than on the raw layer, so a marker standing on a barrow stands on the barrow.
exteriors.limits: Schematic footprints, not measured art: plot and dimension metres are sized for legibility and every part is a placeholder identity. Ground elevation is bilinear over the height layer, because the generator own continuous height field is not importable from a reader package - at plot scale on a multi-kilometre raster that is below one cell, so ground_elevation_m and foundation_bottom_m come out near-equal and a consumer should conform plots to its own landscape rather than trust these to describe local relief. Ground shaping is emitted twice over: as parametric primitives, which are exact and are what an engine with its own landscape should apply, and as a sampled surface grid, which is the coarse derived form for a consumer that only reads grids. Where they disagree the primitives are right.

fields.unreached: positive infinity (float("inf")) -- NOT representable in JSON, encode as your own sentinel

seed_digest: sha256 -> first 4 bytes big-endian -> random.Random (CPython MT19937)
method: Archetypes are catalogue data, not code. Each declares the layers it requires, the layers that make one cell better than another, how many of itself belong in a thousand square kilometres of land, and how far apart two may stand. Requirements are percentile-relative to each world own distribution with an absolute floor, so a world with no volcanism gets no lava tubes rather than its least-quiet hillside. Candidates are thinned greedily over jittered suitability with per-archetype and per-family spacing and a clearance from anywhere people already live. Ground already carrying a ruin, nest, shrine, college or landmark is left to the module that placed it. State and occupant are then derived from the surrounding record - a nearby ruin ages a site, remoteness empties it, an unstable weave corrupts it, a nest nearby fills it - and a succession pass lets something else move into what the builders left. Tier 2 sites gain an interior chamber graph.
limits: Static proposals about ground, not a populated world. Nothing here acts, spawns, patrols, guards or holds treasure. Interiors are graphs - depth, role, rough size, connections - with no metre positions, no contents and no encounters; a real interior layout is a later phase. Tier is physical scale and how much the place still needs building out, never danger: read threat for that. T0 chain furniture (waystones, boundary stones, beacon lines) is not placed yet and arrives with the composition pass.
